segs.e: Linked Discourses 36.1
1. With Verses
Immersion
“Mendicants, there are these three feelings.
What three?

segs.p: Sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā—
segs.e: Pleasant, painful, and neutral feeling.
These are the three feelings.
Stilled, aware,
a mindful disciple of the Buddha
understands feelings,
the cause of feelings,
where they cease,
and the path that leads to their ending.
With the ending of feelings, a mendicant
is hungerless, quenched.”
Linked Discourses 36.2
1. With Verses
Pleasure
“Mendicants, there are these three feelings.
What three?

segs.p: Sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā—
segs.e: Pleasant, painful, and neutral feeling.
These are the three feelings.
Whether it’s pleasant or painful,
as well as what’s neutral,
whatever there is that is felt
internally and externally:
having known, ‘this is suffering,
deceptive, breaking apart’,
seeing feelings vanish with every contact,
that’s how they become free of desire for them.”
Linked Discourses 36.3
1. With Verses
Giving Up
“Mendicants, there are these three feelings.
What three?

segs.p: Sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā.
segs.e: Pleasant, painful, and neutral feeling.

segs.p: Sukhāya, bhikkhave, vedanāya rāgānusayo pahātabbo, dukkhāya vedanāya paṭighānusayo pahātabbo, adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya avijjānusayo pahātabbo.
segs.e: The underlying tendency to greed should be given up when it comes to pleasant feeling. The underlying tendency to aversion should be given up when it comes to painful feeling. The underlying tendency to ignorance should be given up when it comes to neutral feeling.

segs.p: Yato kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno sukhāya vedanāya rāgānusayo pahīno hoti, dukkhāya vedanāya paṭighānusayo pahīno hoti, adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya avijjānusayo pahīno hoti, ayaṁ vuccati, bhikkhave, ‘bhikkhu niranusayo sammaddaso acchecchi taṇhaṁ, vivattayi saṁyojanaṁ, sammā mānābhisamayā antamakāsi dukkhassā’ti.
segs.e: When a mendicant has given up these underlying tendencies, they’re called a mendicant without underlying tendencies, who sees rightly, has cut off craving, cast off the fetters, and by rightly comprehending conceit has made an end of suffering.
When you feel pleasure
without understanding feeling,
the underlying tendency to greed is there,
if you don’t see the escape.
When you feel pain
without understanding feeling,
the underlying tendency to aversion is there,
if you don’t see the escape.
As for that peaceful, neutral feeling:
he of vast wisdom has taught
that if you relish it,
you’re still not released from suffering.
But when a mendicant is keen,
not neglecting situational awareness,
that astute person
understands all feelings.
Completely understanding feelings,
they’re without defilements in this very life.
That knowledge master is firm in principle;
when their body breaks up, they can’t be reckoned.”
Linked Discourses 36.4
1. With Verses
The Abyss
“Mendicants, when an unlearned ordinary person says that
there’s an abyss under the ocean,

segs.p: Taṁ kho panetaṁ, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano asantaṁ avijjamānaṁ evaṁ vācaṁ bhāsati:
segs.e: they’re speaking of something that doesn’t exist.

segs.p: Sārīrikānaṁ kho etaṁ, bhikkhave, dukkhānaṁ vedanānaṁ adhivacanaṁ yadidaṁ ‘pātālo’ti.
segs.e: ‘Abyss’ is a term for painful physical feelings.

segs.p: Assutavā, bhikkhave, puthujjano sārīrikāya dukkhāya vedanāya phuṭṭho samāno socati kilamati paridevati urattāḷiṁ kandati sammohaṁ āpajjati.
segs.e: When an unlearned ordinary person experiences painful physical feelings they sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion.

segs.p: Ayaṁ vuccati, bhikkhave, ‘assutavā puthujjano pātāle na paccuṭṭhāsi, gādhañca nājjhagā’.
segs.e: They’re called an unlearned ordinary person who hasn’t stood up in the abyss and has found no footing.

segs.p: Sutavā ca kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako sārīrikāya dukkhāya vedanāya phuṭṭho samāno neva socati, na kilamati, na paridevati, na urattāḷiṁ kandati, na sammohaṁ āpajjati.
segs.e: When a learned noble disciple experiences painful physical feelings they don’t sorrow or wail or lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion.

segs.p: Ayaṁ vuccati, bhikkhave, ‘sutavā ariyasāvako pātāle paccuṭṭhāsi, gādhañca ajjhagā’ti.
segs.e: They’re called a learned noble disciple who has stood up in the abyss and found a footing.
If you can’t abide
those painful physical feelings
that arise and sap your vitality;
if you tremble at their touch,
weeping and wailing,
a weakling lacking strength—
you won’t stand up in the abyss
and find a footing.
If you can endure
those painful physical feelings
that arise and sap your vitality;
if you don’t tremble at their touch—
you stand up in the abyss
and find a footing.”
Linked Discourses 36.5
1. With Verses
Should Be Seen
“Mendicants, there are these three feelings.
What three?

segs.p: Sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā.
segs.e: Pleasant, painful, and neutral feeling.

segs.p: Sukhā, bhikkhave, vedanā dukkhato daṭṭhabbā, dukkhā vedanā sallato daṭṭhabbā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā aniccato daṭṭhabbā.
segs.e: Pleasant feeling should be seen as suffering. Painful feeling should be seen as a dart. Neutral feeling should be seen as impermanent.

segs.p: Yato kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno sukhā vedanā dukkhato diṭṭhā hoti, dukkhā vedanā sallato diṭṭhā hoti, adukkhamasukhā vedanā aniccato diṭṭhā hoti—
segs.e: When a mendicant has seen these three feelings in this way,

segs.p: ayaṁ vuccati, bhikkhave, ‘bhikkhu sammaddaso acchecchi taṇhaṁ, vivattayi saṁyojanaṁ, sammā mānābhisamayā antamakāsi dukkhassā’ti.
segs.e: they’re called a mendicant who sees rightly, has cut off craving, cast off the fetters, and by rightly comprehending conceit has made an end of suffering.
A mendicant who sees pleasure as pain,
and suffering as a dart,
and that peaceful, neutral feeling
as impermanent
sees rightly;
they completely understand feelings.
Completely understanding feelings,
they’re without defilements in this very life.
That knowledge master is firm in principle;
when their body breaks up, they can’t be reckoned.”
Linked Discourses 36.6
1. With Verses
An Arrow

segs.p: “Assutavā, bhikkhave, puthujjano sukhampi vedanaṁ vedayati, dukkhampi vedanaṁ vedayati, adukkhamasukhampi vedanaṁ vedayati.
segs.e: “Mendicants, an unlearned ordinary person feels pleasant, painful, and neutral feelings.

segs.p: Sutavā, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako sukhampi vedanaṁ vedayati, dukkhampi vedanaṁ vedayati, adukkhamasukhampi vedanaṁ vedayati.
segs.e: A learned noble disciple also feels pleasant, painful, and neutral feelings.

segs.p: Tatra, bhikkhave, ko viseso ko adhippayāso kiṁ nānākaraṇaṁ sutavato ariyasāvakassa assutavatā puthujjanenā”ti?
segs.e: What, then, is the difference between a learned noble disciple and an ordinary unlearned person?”
“Our teachings are rooted in the Buddha. …”

segs.p: assutavā, bhikkhave, puthujjano dukkhāya vedanāya phuṭṭho samāno socati kilamati paridevati urattāḷiṁ kandati sammohaṁ āpajjati.
segs.e: “When an unlearned ordinary person experiences painful physical feelings they sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion.
They experience two feelings:
physical and mental.
It’s like a person who is struck with an arrow,
only to be struck with a second arrow.

segs.p: Evañhi so, bhikkhave, puriso dvisallena vedanaṁ vedayati.
segs.e: That person experiences the feeling of two arrows.

segs.p: Evameva kho, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano dukkhāya vedanāya phuṭṭho samāno socati kilamati paridevati urattāḷiṁ kandati sammohaṁ āpajjati.
segs.e: In the same way, when an unlearned ordinary person experiences painful physical feelings they sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion.
They experience two feelings:
physical and mental.

segs.p: Tassāyeva kho pana dukkhāya vedanāya phuṭṭho samāno paṭighavā hoti.
segs.e: When they’re touched by painful feeling, they resist it.

segs.p: Tamenaṁ dukkhāya vedanāya paṭighavantaṁ, yo dukkhāya vedanāya paṭighānusayo, so anuseti.
segs.e: The underlying tendency for aversion toward painful feeling underlies that.

segs.p: So dukkhāya vedanāya phuṭṭho samāno kāmasukhaṁ abhinandati.
segs.e: When touched by painful feeling they look forward to enjoying sensual pleasures.
Why is that?

segs.p: Na hi so, bhikkhave, pajānāti assutavā puthujjano aññatra kāmasukhā dukkhāya vedanāya nissaraṇaṁ,
segs.e: Because an unlearned ordinary person doesn’t understand any escape from painful feeling apart from sensual pleasures.

segs.p: tassa kāmasukhañca abhinandato, yo sukhāya vedanāya rāgānusayo, so anuseti.
segs.e: Since they look forward to enjoying sensual pleasures, the underlying tendency to greed for pleasant feeling underlies that.

segs.p: So tāsaṁ vedanānaṁ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṁ nappajānāti.
segs.e: They don’t truly understand feelings’ origin, disappearance, gratification, drawback, and escape.

segs.p: Tassa tāsaṁ vedanānaṁ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṁ appajānato, yo adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya avijjānusayo, so anuseti.
segs.e: The underlying tendency to ignorance about neutral feeling underlies that.

segs.p: So sukhañce vedanaṁ vedayati, saññutto naṁ vedayati.
segs.e: If they feel a pleasant feeling, they feel it attached.

segs.p: Dukkhañce vedanaṁ vedayati, saññutto naṁ vedayati.
segs.e: If they feel a painful feeling, they feel it attached.

segs.p: Adukkhamasukhañce vedanaṁ vedayati, saññutto naṁ vedayati.
segs.e: If they feel a neutral feeling, they feel it attached.

segs.p: Ayaṁ vuccati, bhikkhave, ‘assutavā puthujjano saññutto jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi, saññutto dukkhasmā’ti vadāmi.
segs.e: They’re called an unlearned ordinary person who is attached to rebirth, old age, and death, to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. They are attached to suffering, I say.

segs.p: Sutavā ca kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako dukkhāya vedanāya phuṭṭho samāno na socati, na kilamati, na paridevati, na urattāḷiṁ kandati, na sammohaṁ āpajjati.
segs.e: When a learned noble disciple experiences painful physical feelings they don’t sorrow or wail or lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion.
They experience one feeling:
physical, not mental.
It’s like a person who is struck with an arrow,

segs.p: Tamenaṁ dutiyena sallena anuvedhaṁ na vijjheyya.
segs.e: but was not struck with a second arrow.

segs.p: Evañhi so, bhikkhave, puriso ekasallena vedanaṁ vedayati.
segs.e: That person would experience the feeling of one arrow.

segs.p: Evameva kho, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako dukkhāya vedanāya phuṭṭho samāno na socati, na kilamati, na paridevati, na urattāḷiṁ kandati, na sammohaṁ āpajjati.
segs.e: In the same way, when a learned noble disciple experiences painful physical feelings they don’t sorrow or wail or lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion.
They experience one feeling:
physical, not mental.

segs.p: Tassāyeva kho pana dukkhāya vedanāya phuṭṭho samāno paṭighavā na hoti.
segs.e: When they’re touched by painful feeling, they don’t resist it.

segs.p: Tamenaṁ dukkhāya vedanāya appaṭighavantaṁ, yo dukkhāya vedanāya paṭighānusayo, so nānuseti.
segs.e: There’s no underlying tendency for aversion toward painful feeling underlying that.

segs.p: So dukkhāya vedanāya phuṭṭho samāno kāmasukhaṁ nābhinandati.
segs.e: When touched by painful feeling they don’t look forward to enjoying sensual pleasures.
Why is that?

segs.p: Pajānāti hi so, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako aññatra kāmasukhā dukkhāya vedanāya nissaraṇaṁ.
segs.e: Because a learned noble disciple understands an escape from painful feeling apart from sensual pleasures.

segs.p: Tassa kāmasukhaṁ nābhinandato yo sukhāya vedanāya rāgānusayo, so nānuseti.
segs.e: Since they don’t look forward to enjoying sensual pleasures, there’s no underlying tendency to greed for pleasant feeling underlying that.

segs.p: So tāsaṁ vedanānaṁ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavaṁ ca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṁ pajānāti.
segs.e: They truly understand feelings’ origin, disappearance, gratification, drawback, and escape.

segs.p: Tassa tāsaṁ vedanānaṁ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṁ pajānato, yo adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya avijjānusayo, so nānuseti.
segs.e: There’s no underlying tendency to ignorance about neutral feeling underlying that.

segs.p: So sukhañce vedanaṁ vedayati, visaññutto naṁ vedayati.
segs.e: If they feel a pleasant feeling, they feel it detached.

segs.p: Dukkhañce vedanaṁ vedayati, visaññutto naṁ vedayati.
segs.e: If they feel a painful feeling, they feel it detached.

segs.p: Adukkhamasukhañce vedanaṁ vedayati, visaññutto naṁ vedayati.
segs.e: If they feel a neutral feeling, they feel it detached.

segs.p: Ayaṁ vuccati, bhikkhave, ‘sutavā ariyasāvako visaññutto jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi, visaññutto dukkhasmā’ti vadāmi.
segs.e: They’re called a learned noble disciple who is detached from rebirth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. They are detached from suffering, I say.

segs.p: Ayaṁ kho, bhikkhave, viseso, ayaṁ adhippayāso, idaṁ nānākaraṇaṁ sutavato ariyasāvakassa assutavatā puthujjanenāti.
segs.e: This is the difference between a learned noble disciple and an unlearned ordinary person.
A wise and learned person does not not feel
the feeling of pleasure and pain.
This is the great difference of skill
between the attentive one and the ordinary.
A learned person who has appraised the teaching
discerns this world and the next.
Desirable things don’t disturb their mind,
nor are they repelled by the undesirable.
Both favoring and opposing
are cleared and ended, and are no more.
Knowing the stainless, sorrowless state,
they who have gone beyond rebirth <j>understand rightly.”
Linked Discourses 36.7
1. With Verses
The Infirmary (1st)

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā vesāliyaṁ viharati mahāvane kūṭāgārasālāyaṁ.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā sāyanhasamayaṁ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yena gilānasālā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi.
segs.e: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat and went to the infirmary, where he sat down on the seat spread out,
and addressed the mendicants:
“Mendicants, a mendicant should await their time mindful and aware.
This is my instruction to you.
And how is a mendicant mindful?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṁ;
segs.e: It’s when a mendicant meditates by observing an aspect of the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.
They meditate observing an aspect of feelings …
They meditate observing an aspect of the mind …

segs.p: dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṁ.
segs.e: They meditate observing an aspect of principles—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world.

segs.p: Evaṁ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sato hoti.
segs.e: That’s how a mendicant is mindful.
And how is a mendicant aware?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu abhikkante paṭikkante sampajānakārī hoti, ālokite vilokite sampajānakārī hoti, samiñjite pasārite sampajānakārī hoti, saṅghāṭipattacīvaradhāraṇe sampajānakārī hoti, asite pīte khāyite sāyite sampajānakārī hoti, uccārapassāvakamme sampajānakārī hoti, gate ṭhite nisinne sutte jāgarite bhāsite tuṇhībhāve sampajānakārī hoti.
segs.e: It’s when a mendicant acts with situational awareness when going out and coming back; when looking ahead and aside; when bending and extending the limbs; when bearing the outer robe, bowl and robes; when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; when urinating and defecating; when walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and keeping silent.

segs.p: Evaṁ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sampajānakārī hoti.
segs.e: That’s how a mendicant acts with situational awareness.

segs.p: Sato, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sampajāno kālaṁ āgameyya.
segs.e: A mendicant should await their time mindful and aware.
This is my instruction to you.

segs.p: Tassa ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno evaṁ satassa sampajānassa appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato uppajjati sukhā vedanā, so evaṁ pajānāti:
segs.e: While a mendicant is meditating like this—mindful, aware, diligent, keen, and resolute—if pleasant feelings arise, they understand:
‘A pleasant feeling has arisen in me.

segs.p: Sā ca kho paṭicca, no appaṭicca.
segs.e: That’s dependent, not independent.
Dependent on what?
Dependent on my own body.

segs.p: Ayaṁ kho pana kāyo anicco saṅkhato paṭiccasamuppanno.
segs.e: But this body is impermanent, conditioned, dependently originated.

segs.p: Aniccaṁ kho pana saṅkhataṁ paṭiccasamuppannaṁ kāyaṁ paṭicca uppannā sukhā vedanā kuto niccā bhavissatī’ti.
segs.e: So how could a pleasant feeling be permanent, since it has arisen dependent on a body that is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently originated?’

segs.p: So kāye ca sukhāya ca vedanāya aniccānupassī viharati, vayānupassī viharati, virāgānupassī viharati, nirodhānupassī viharati, paṭinissaggānupassī viharati.
segs.e: They meditate observing impermanence, vanishing, dispassion, cessation, and letting go in the body and pleasant feeling.

segs.p: Tassa kāye ca sukhāya ca vedanāya aniccānupassino viharato, vayānupassino viharato, virāgānupassino viharato, nirodhānupassino viharato, paṭinissaggānupassino viharato, yo kāye ca sukhāya ca vedanāya rāgānusayo, so pahīyati.
segs.e: As they do so, they give up the underlying tendency to greed for the body and pleasant feeling.

segs.p: Tassa ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno evaṁ satassa sampajānassa appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato uppajjati dukkhā vedanā.
segs.e: While a mendicant is meditating like this—mindful, aware, diligent, keen, and resolute—if painful feelings arise, they understand:
‘A painful feeling has arisen in me.

segs.p: Sā ca kho paṭicca, no appaṭicca.
segs.e: That’s dependent, not independent.
Dependent on what?
Dependent on my own body.

segs.p: Ayaṁ kho pana kāyo anicco saṅkhato paṭiccasamuppanno.
segs.e: But this body is impermanent, conditioned, dependently originated.

segs.p: Aniccaṁ kho pana saṅkhataṁ paṭiccasamuppannaṁ kāyaṁ paṭicca uppannā dukkhā vedanā kuto niccā bhavissatī’ti.
segs.e: So how could a painful feeling be permanent, since it has arisen dependent on a body that is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently originated?’

segs.p: So kāye ca dukkhāya ca vedanāya aniccānupassī viharati, vayānupassī viharati, virāgānupassī viharati, nirodhānupassī viharati, paṭinissaggānupassī viharati.
segs.e: They meditate observing impermanence, vanishing, dispassion, cessation, and letting go in the body and painful feeling.

segs.p: Tassa kāye ca dukkhāya ca vedanāya aniccānupassino viharato …pe… paṭinissaggānupassino viharato, yo kāye ca dukkhāya ca vedanāya paṭighānusayo, so pahīyati.
segs.e: As they do so, they give up the underlying tendency to aversion toward the body and painful feeling.

segs.p: Tassa ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno evaṁ satassa sampajānassa appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato uppajjati adukkhamasukhā vedanā, so evaṁ pajānāti:
segs.e: While a mendicant is meditating like this—mindful, aware, diligent, keen, and resolute—if neutral feelings arise, they understand:
‘A neutral feeling has arisen in me.

segs.p: Sā ca kho paṭicca, no appaṭicca.
segs.e: That’s dependent, not independent.
Dependent on what?
Dependent on my own body.

segs.p: Ayaṁ kho pana kāyo anicco saṅkhato paṭiccasamuppanno.
segs.e: But this body is impermanent, conditioned, dependently originated.

segs.p: Aniccaṁ kho pana saṅkhataṁ paṭiccasamuppannaṁ kāyaṁ paṭicca uppannā adukkhamasukhā vedanā kuto niccā bhavissatī’ti.
segs.e: So how could a neutral feeling be permanent, since it has arisen dependent on a body that is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently originated?’

segs.p: So kāye ca adukkhamasukhāya ca vedanāya aniccānupassī viharati, vayānupassī viharati, virāgānupassī viharati, nirodhānupassī viharati, paṭinissaggānupassī viharati.
segs.e: They meditate observing impermanence, vanishing, dispassion, cessation, and letting go in the body and neutral feeling.

segs.p: Tassa kāye ca adukkhamasukhāya ca vedanāya aniccānupassino viharato …pe… paṭinissaggānupassino viharato, yo kāye ca adukkhamasukhāya ca vedanāya avijjānusayo, so pahīyati.
segs.e: As they do so, they give up the underlying tendency to ignorance toward the body and neutral feeling.

segs.p: So sukhañce vedanaṁ vedayati, sā aniccāti pajānāti, anajjhositāti pajānāti, anabhinanditāti pajānāti;
segs.e: If they feel a pleasant feeling, they understand that it’s impermanent, that they’re not attached to it, and that they don’t take pleasure in it.
If they feel a painful feeling, they understand that it’s impermanent, that they’re not attached to it, and that they don’t take pleasure in it.

segs.p: adukkhamasukhañce vedanaṁ vedayati, sā aniccāti pajānāti, anajjhositāti pajānāti, anabhinanditāti pajānāti.
segs.e: If they feel a neutral feeling, they understand that it’s impermanent, that they’re not attached to it, and that they don’t take pleasure in it.

segs.p: So sukhañce vedanaṁ vedayati, visaññutto naṁ vedayati;
segs.e: If they feel a pleasant feeling, they feel it detached.

segs.p: dukkhañce vedanaṁ vedayati, visaññutto naṁ vedayati;
segs.e: If they feel a painful feeling, they feel it detached.

segs.p: adukkhamasukhañce vedanaṁ vedayati, visaññutto naṁ vedayati.
segs.e: If they feel a neutral feeling, they feel it detached.

segs.p: So kāyapariyantikaṁ vedanaṁ vedayamāno ‘kāyapariyantikaṁ vedanaṁ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti, jīvitapariyantikaṁ vedanaṁ vedayamāno ‘jīvitapariyantikaṁ vedanaṁ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti.
segs.e: Feeling the end of the body draw close, they understand: ‘I feel the end of the body draw close.’ Feeling the end of life draw close, they understand: ‘I feel the end of life draw close.’

segs.p: ‘Kāyassa bhedā uddhaṁ jīvitapariyādānā idheva sabbavedayitāni anabhinanditāni sītībhavissantī’ti pajānāti.
segs.e: They understand: ‘When my body breaks up and my life has come to an end, everything that’s felt, since I no longer take pleasure in it, will become cool right here.’

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, telañca paṭicca vaṭṭiñca paṭicca telappadīpo jhāyeyya,
segs.e: Suppose an oil lamp depended on oil and a wick to burn.

segs.p: tasseva telassa ca vaṭṭiyā ca pariyādānā anāhāro nibbāyeyya;
segs.e: As the oil and the wick are used up, it would be extinguished due to not being fed.

segs.p: evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāyapariyantikaṁ vedanaṁ vedayamāno ‘kāyapariyantikaṁ vedanaṁ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti. Jīvitapariyantikaṁ vedanaṁ vedayamāno ‘jīvitapariyantikaṁ vedanaṁ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti.
segs.e: In the same way, feeling the end of the body draw close, a mendicant understands: ‘I feel the end of the body draw close.’ Feeling the end of life draw close, a mendicant understands: ‘I feel the end of life draw close.’

segs.p: ‘Kāyassa bhedā uddhaṁ jīvitapariyādānā idheva sabbavedayitāni anabhinanditāni sītībhavissantī’ti pajānātī”ti.

segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.

Linked Discourses 36.9
1. With Verses
Impermanent

segs.p: “Tisso imā, bhikkhave, vedanā aniccā saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā khayadhammā vayadhammā virāgadhammā nirodhadhammā.
segs.e: “Mendicants, these three feelings are impermanent, conditioned, dependently originated, liable to end, vanish, fade away, and cease.
What three?

segs.p: Sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā—
segs.e: Pleasant, painful, and neutral feeling.

segs.p: imā kho, bhikkhave, tisso vedanā aniccā saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā khayadhammā vayadhammā virāgadhammā nirodhadhammā”ti.
segs.e: These are the three feelings that are impermanent, conditioned, dependently originated, liable to end, vanish, fade away, and cease.”
Linked Discourses 36.10
1. With Verses
Rooted in Contact

segs.p: “Tisso imā, bhikkhave, vedanā phassajā phassamūlakā phassanidānā phassapaccayā.
segs.e: “Mendicants, these three feelings are born, rooted, sourced, and dependent on contact.
What three?

segs.p: Sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā.
segs.e: Pleasant, painful, and neutral feeling.

segs.p: Sukhavedaniyaṁ, bhikkhave, phassaṁ paṭicca uppajjati sukhā vedanā.
segs.e: Pleasant feeling arises dependent on a contact to be experienced as pleasant.

segs.p: Tasseva sukhavedaniyassa phassassa nirodhā, yaṁ tajjaṁ vedayitaṁ sukhavedaniyaṁ phassaṁ paṭicca uppannā sukhā vedanā, sā nirujjhati, sā vūpasammati.
segs.e: With the cessation of that contact to be experienced as pleasant, the corresponding pleasant feeling ceases and stops.

segs.p: Dukkhavedaniyaṁ, bhikkhave, phassaṁ paṭicca uppajjati dukkhā vedanā.
segs.e: Painful feeling arises dependent on a contact to be experienced as painful.

segs.p: Tasseva dukkhavedaniyassa phassassa nirodhā, yaṁ tajjaṁ vedayitaṁ dukkhavedaniyaṁ phassaṁ paṭicca uppannā dukkhā vedanā, sā nirujjhati, sā vūpasammati.
segs.e: With the cessation of that contact to be experienced as painful, the corresponding painful feeling ceases and stops.

segs.p: Adukkhamasukhavedaniyaṁ, bhikkhave, phassaṁ paṭicca uppajjati adukkhamasukhā vedanā.
segs.e: Neutral feeling arises dependent on a contact to be experienced as neutral.

segs.p: Tasseva adukkhamasukhavedaniyassa phassassa nirodhā, yaṁ tajjaṁ vedayitaṁ adukkhamasukhavedaniyaṁ phassaṁ paṭicca uppannā adukkhamasukhā vedanā, sā nirujjhati, sā vūpasammati.
segs.e: With the cessation of that contact to be experienced as neutral, the corresponding neutral feeling ceases and stops.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, dvinnaṁ kaṭṭhānaṁ saṅghaṭṭanasamodhānā usmā jāyati, tejo abhinibbattati. Tesaṁyeva kaṭṭhānaṁ nānābhāvā vinikkhepā, yā tajjā usmā, sā nirujjhati, sā vūpasammati.
segs.e: When you rub two sticks together, heat is generated and fire is produced. But when you part the sticks and lay them aside, any corresponding heat ceases and stops.

segs.p: Evameva kho, bhikkhave, imā tisso vedanā phassajā phassamūlakā phassanidānā phassapaccayā.
segs.e: In the same way, these three feelings are born, rooted, sourced, and dependent on contact.

segs.p: Tajjaṁ phassaṁ paṭicca tajjā vedanā uppajjanti.
segs.e: The appropriate feeling arises dependent on the corresponding contact.

segs.p: Tajjassa phassassa nirodhā tajjā vedanā nirujjhantī”ti.
segs.e: When the corresponding contact ceases, the appropriate feeling ceases.”
Linked Discourses 36.11
2. In Private
In Private

segs.p: Atha kho aññataro bhikkhu yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho so bhikkhu bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then a mendicant went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

segs.p: “idha mayhaṁ, bhante, rahogatassa paṭisallīnassa evaṁ cetaso parivitakko udapādi—
segs.e: “Just now, sir, as I was in private retreat this thought came to mind.
The Buddha has spoken of three feelings.

segs.p: Sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā—
segs.e: Pleasant, painful, and neutral feeling.
These are the three feelings the Buddha has spoken of.
But the Buddha has also said:
‘Suffering includes whatever is felt.’

segs.p: Kiṁ nu kho etaṁ bhagavatā sandhāya bhāsitaṁ:
segs.e: What was the Buddha referring to when he said this?”
“Good, good, mendicant!

segs.p: Tisso imā, bhikkhu, vedanā vuttā mayā.
segs.e: I have spoken of these three feelings.

segs.p: Sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā—
segs.e: Pleasant, painful, and neutral feeling.
These are the three feelings I have spoken of.
But I have also said:
‘Suffering includes whatever is felt.’

segs.p: Taṁ kho panetaṁ, bhikkhu, mayā saṅkhārānaṁyeva aniccataṁ sandhāya bhāsitaṁ:
segs.e: When I said this I was referring to the impermanence of conditions, to the fact that conditions are

segs.p: Taṁ kho panetaṁ, bhikkhu, mayā saṅkhārānaṁyeva khayadhammataṁ …pe…
segs.e: liable to end,
vanish,
fade away,
cease,
and perish.

segs.p: Atha kho pana, bhikkhu, mayā anupubbasaṅkhārānaṁ nirodho akkhāto.
segs.e: But I have also explained the progressive cessation of activities.

segs.p: Paṭhamaṁ jhānaṁ samāpannassa vācā niruddhā hoti.
segs.e: For someone who has attained the first absorption, speech has ceased.

segs.p: Dutiyaṁ jhānaṁ samāpannassa vitakkavicārā niruddhā honti.
segs.e: For someone who has attained the second absorption, the placing of the mind and keeping it connected have ceased.

segs.p: Tatiyaṁ jhānaṁ samāpannassa pīti niruddhā hoti.
segs.e: For someone who has attained the third absorption, rapture has ceased.

segs.p: Catutthaṁ jhānaṁ samāpannassa assāsapassāsā niruddhā honti.
segs.e: For someone who has attained the fourth absorption, breathing has ceased.
For someone who has attained the dimension of infinite space, the perception of form has ceased.
For someone who has attained the dimension of infinite consciousness, the perception of the dimension of infinite space has ceased.
For someone who has attained the dimension of nothingness, the perception of the dimension of infinite consciousness has ceased.
For someone who has attained the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, the perception of the dimension of nothingness has ceased.

segs.p: Saññāvedayitanirodhaṁ samāpannassa saññā ca vedanā ca niruddhā honti.
segs.e: For someone who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, perception and feeling have ceased.

segs.p: Khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno rāgo niruddho hoti, doso niruddho hoti, moho niruddho hoti.
segs.e: For a mendicant who has ended the defilements, greed, hate, and delusion have ceased.

segs.p: Atha kho, bhikkhu, mayā anupubbasaṅkhārānaṁ vūpasamo akkhāto.
segs.e: And I have also explained the progressive settling of activities.

segs.p: Paṭhamaṁ jhānaṁ samāpannassa vācā vūpasantā hoti.
segs.e: For someone who has attained the first absorption, speech has stilled.

segs.p: Dutiyaṁ jhānaṁ samāpannassa vitakkavicārā vūpasantā honti …pe…
segs.e: For someone who has attained the second absorption, the placing of the mind and keeping it connected have stilled. …

segs.p: saññāvedayitanirodhaṁ samāpannassa saññā ca vedanā ca vūpasantā honti.
segs.e: For someone who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, perception and feeling have stilled.

segs.p: Khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno rāgo vūpasanto hoti, doso vūpasanto hoti, moho vūpasanto hoti.
segs.e: For a mendicant who has ended the defilements, greed, hate, and delusion have stilled.
There are these six levels of tranquility.

segs.p: Paṭhamaṁ jhānaṁ samāpannassa vācā paṭippassaddhā hoti.
segs.e: For someone who has attained the first absorption, speech has been tranquilized.

segs.p: Dutiyaṁ jhānaṁ samāpannassa vitakkavicārā paṭippassaddhā honti.
segs.e: For someone who has attained the second absorption, the placing of the mind and keeping it connected have been tranquilized.

segs.p: Tatiyaṁ jhānaṁ samāpannassa pīti paṭippassaddhā hoti.
segs.e: For someone who has attained the third absorption, rapture has been tranquilized.

segs.p: Catutthaṁ jhānaṁ samāpannassa assāsapassāsā paṭippassaddhā honti.
segs.e: For someone who has attained the fourth absorption, breathing has been tranquilized.

segs.p: Saññāvedayitanirodhaṁ samāpannassa saññā ca vedanā ca paṭippassaddhā honti.
segs.e: For someone who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, perception and feeling have been tranquilized.

segs.p: Khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno rāgo paṭippassaddho hoti, doso paṭippassaddho hoti, moho paṭippassaddho hotī”ti.
segs.e: For a mendicant who has ended the defilements, greed, hate, and delusion have been tranquilized.”
Linked Discourses 36.12
2. In Private
In the Atmosphere (1st)
“Mendicants, various winds blow in the atmosphere.

segs.p: Puratthimāpi vātā vāyanti, pacchimāpi vātā vāyanti, uttarāpi vātā vāyanti, dakkhiṇāpi vātā vāyanti, sarajāpi vātā vāyanti, arajāpi vātā vāyanti, sītāpi vātā vāyanti, uṇhāpi vātā vāyanti, parittāpi vātā vāyanti, adhimattāpi vātā vāyanti.
segs.e: Winds blow from the east, the west, the north, and the south. There are winds that are dusty and dustless, cool and warm, weak and strong.

segs.p: Evameva kho, bhikkhave, imasmiṁ kāyasmiṁ vividhā vedanā uppajjanti, sukhāpi vedanā uppajjati, dukkhāpi vedanā uppajjati, adukkhamasukhāpi vedanā uppajjatīti.
segs.e: In the same way, various feelings arise in this body: pleasant, painful, and neutral feelings.
There are many and various
winds that blow in the atmosphere.
From the east they come, also the west,
the north, and then the south.
They are dusty and dustless,
cool and sometimes warm,
strong and weak;
these are the different gales that blow.
So too, in this body
feelings arise,
pleasant and painful,
and those that are neutral.
But when a mendicant is keen,
not neglecting situational awareness,
that astute person
understands all feelings.
Completely understanding feelings,
they’re without defilements in this very life.
That knowledge master is firm in principle;
when their body breaks up, they can’t be reckoned.”

2. In Private
A Guest House

segs.p: “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, āgantukāgāraṁ. Tattha puratthimāyapi disāya āgantvā vāsaṁ kappenti, pacchimāyapi disāya āgantvā vāsaṁ kappenti, uttarāyapi disāya āgantvā vāsaṁ kappenti, dakkhiṇāyapi disāya āgantvā vāsaṁ kappenti. Khattiyāpi āgantvā vāsaṁ kappenti, brāhmaṇāpi āgantvā vāsaṁ kappenti, vessāpi āgantvā vāsaṁ kappenti, suddāpi āgantvā vāsaṁ kappenti.
segs.e: “Mendicants, suppose there was a guest house. Lodgers come from the east, west, north, and south. Aristocrats, brahmins, peasants, and menials all stay there.

segs.p: Evameva kho, bhikkhave, imasmiṁ kāyasmiṁ vividhā vedanā uppajjanti. Sukhāpi vedanā uppajjati, dukkhāpi vedanā uppajjati, adukkhamasukhāpi vedanā uppajjati.
segs.e: In the same way, various feelings arise in this body: pleasant, painful, and neutral feelings.

segs.p: Sāmisāpi sukhā vedanā uppajjati, sāmisāpi dukkhā vedanā uppajjati, sāmisāpi adukkhamasukhā vedanā uppajjati.
segs.e: Also pleasant, painful, and neutral feelings of the flesh arise.

segs.p: Nirāmisāpi sukhā vedanā uppajjati, nirāmisāpi dukkhā vedanā uppajjati, nirāmisāpi adukkhamasukhā vedanā uppajjatī”ti.
segs.e: Also pleasant, painful, and neutral feelings not of the flesh arise.”
Linked Discourses 36.15
2. In Private
With Ānanda (1st)

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā ānando yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi, ekamantaṁ nisinno kho āyasmā ānando bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then Venerable Ānanda went up to the Buddha … sat down to one side, and said to him:

segs.p: “katamā nu kho, bhante, vedanā, katamo vedanāsamudayo, katamo vedanānirodho, katamā vedanānirodhagāminī paṭipadā?
segs.e: “Sir, what is feeling? What’s the origin of feeling? What’s the cessation of feeling? What’s the practice that leads to the cessation of feeling?

segs.p: Ko vedanāya assādo, ko ādīnavo, kiṁ nissaraṇan”ti?
segs.e: And what is feeling’s gratification, drawback, and escape?”
“Ānanda, there are these three feelings:

segs.p: sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā—
segs.e: pleasant, painful, and neutral.
These are called feelings.
Feeling originates from contact.
When contact ceases, feeling ceases.

segs.p: Ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo vedanānirodhagāminī paṭipadā, seyyathidaṁ—
segs.e: The practice that leads to the cessation of feelings is simply this noble eightfold path, that is:
right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion.

segs.p: Yaṁ vedanaṁ paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṁ somanassaṁ, ayaṁ vedanāya assādo.
segs.e: The pleasure and happiness that arise from feeling: this is its gratification.

segs.p: Yaṁ vedanā aniccā dukkhā vipariṇāmadhammā, ayaṁ vedanāya ādīnavo.
segs.e: That feeling is impermanent, suffering, and perishable: this is its drawback.

segs.p: Yo vedanāya chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānaṁ, idaṁ vedanāya nissaraṇaṁ.
segs.e: Removing and giving up desire and greed for feeling: this is its escape.

segs.p: Atha kho panānanda, mayā anupubbasaṅkhārānaṁ nirodho akkhāto.
segs.e: But I have also explained the progressive cessation of activities.

segs.p: Paṭhamaṁ jhānaṁ samāpannassa vācā niruddhā hoti …pe…
segs.e: For someone who has attained the first absorption, speech has ceased. …

segs.p: saññāvedayitanirodhaṁ samāpannassa saññā ca vedanā ca niruddhā honti.
segs.e: For someone who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, perception and feeling have ceased.

segs.p: Khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno rāgo niruddho hoti, doso niruddho hoti, moho niruddho hoti.
segs.e: For a mendicant who has ended the defilements, greed, hate, and delusion have ceased.

segs.p: Atha kho panānanda, mayā anupubbasaṅkhārānaṁ vūpasamo akkhāto.
segs.e: And I have also explained the progressive settling of activities.

segs.p: Paṭhamaṁ jhānaṁ samāpannassa vācā vūpasantā hoti …pe…
segs.e: For someone who has attained the first absorption, speech has stilled. …

segs.p: saññāvedayitanirodhaṁ samāpannassa saññā ca vedanā ca vūpasantā honti.
segs.e: For someone who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, perception and feeling have stilled.

segs.p: Khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno rāgo vūpasanto hoti, doso vūpasanto hoti, moho vūpasanto hoti.
segs.e: For a mendicant who has ended the defilements, greed, hate, and delusion have stilled.

segs.p: Atha kho panānanda, mayā anupubbasaṅkhārānaṁ paṭippassaddhi akkhātā.
segs.e: And I have also explained the progressive tranquilizing of activities.

segs.p: Paṭhamaṁ jhānaṁ samāpannassa vācā paṭippassaddhā hoti …pe…
segs.e: For someone who has attained the first absorption, speech has been tranquilized. …
For someone who has attained the dimension of infinite space, the perception of form has been tranquilized.
For someone who has attained the dimension of infinite consciousness, the perception of the dimension of infinite space has been tranquilized.
For someone who has attained the dimension of nothingness, the perception of the dimension of infinite consciousness has been tranquilized.
For someone who has attained the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, the perception of the dimension of nothingness has been tranquilized.

segs.p: Saññāvedayitanirodhaṁ samāpannassa saññā ca vedanā ca paṭippassaddhā honti.
segs.e: For someone who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, perception and feeling have been tranquilized.

segs.p: Khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno rāgo paṭippassaddho hoti, doso paṭippassaddho hoti, moho paṭippassaddho hotī”ti.
segs.e: For a mendicant who has ended the defilements, greed, hate, and delusion have been tranquilized.”

2. In Private
With Ānanda (2nd)

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā ānando yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinnaṁ kho āyasmantaṁ ānandaṁ bhagavā etadavoca:
segs.e: Then Venerable Ānanda went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him,

segs.p: “katamā nu kho, ānanda, vedanā, katamo vedanāsamudayo, katamo vedanānirodho, katamā vedanānirodhagāminī paṭipadā?
segs.e: “Ānanda, what is feeling? What’s the origin of feeling? What’s the cessation of feeling? What’s the practice that leads to the cessation of feeling?

segs.p: Ko vedanāya assādo, ko ādīnavo, kiṁ nissaraṇan”ti?
segs.e: And what is feeling’s gratification, drawback, and escape?”

segs.p: “Bhagavaṁmūlakā no, bhante, dhammā bhagavaṁnettikā bhagavaṁpaṭisaraṇā. Sādhu, bhante, bhagavantaññeva paṭibhātu etassa bhāsitassa attho. Bhagavato sutvā bhikkhū dhāressantī”ti.
segs.e: “Our teachings are rooted in the Buddha. He is our guide and our refuge. Sir, may the Buddha himself please clarify the meaning of this. The mendicants will listen and remember it.”

segs.p: “Tena hi, ānanda, suṇohi, sādhukaṁ manasi karohi; bhāsissāmī”ti.
segs.e: “Well then, Ānanda, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.”

segs.p: “Evaṁ, bhante”ti kho āyasmā ānando bhagavato paccassosi.
segs.e: “Yes, sir,” Ānanda replied.
The Buddha said this:
“Ānanda, there are these three feelings:

segs.p: sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā—
segs.e: pleasant, painful, and neutral.
These are called feelings. …

segs.p: khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno rāgo paṭippassaddho hoti, doso paṭippassaddho hoti, moho paṭippassaddho hotī”ti.
segs.e: For a mendicant who has ended the defilements, greed, hate, and delusion have been tranquilized.”

With Several Mendicants (1st)

segs.p: Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdiṁsu. Ekamantaṁ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṁ etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: Then several mendicants went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

segs.p: “katamā nu kho, bhante, vedanā, katamo vedanāsamudayo, katamo vedanānirodho, katamā vedanānirodhagāminī paṭipadā?
segs.e: “Sir, what is feeling? What’s the origin of feeling? What’s the cessation of feeling? What’s the practice that leads to the cessation of feeling?

segs.p: Ko vedanāya assādo, ko ādīnavo, kiṁ nissaraṇan”ti?
segs.e: And what is feeling’s gratification, drawback, and escape?”
“Mendicants, there are these three feelings:

segs.p: sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā—
segs.e: pleasant, painful, and neutral.
These are called feelings.
Feeling originates from contact.
When contact ceases, feeling ceases.

segs.p: Ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo vedanānirodhagāminī paṭipadā, seyyathidaṁ—
segs.e: The practice that leads to the cessation of feelings is simply this noble eightfold path, that is:
right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion.

segs.p: Yaṁ vedanaṁ paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṁ somanassaṁ, ayaṁ vedanāya assādo.
segs.e: The pleasure and happiness that arise from feeling: this is its gratification.

segs.p: Yaṁ vedanā aniccā dukkhā vipariṇāmadhammā, ayaṁ vedanāya ādīnavo.
segs.e: That feeling is impermanent, suffering, and perishable: this is its drawback.

segs.p: Yo vedanāya chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānaṁ, idaṁ vedanāya nissaraṇaṁ.
segs.e: Removing and giving up desire and greed for feeling: this is its escape.

segs.p: Atha kho pana, bhikkhave, mayā anupubbasaṅkhārānaṁ nirodho akkhāto.
segs.e: But I have also explained the progressive cessation of activities. …

segs.p: Paṭhamaṁ jhānaṁ samāpannassa vācā niruddhā hoti …pe…
segs.e: For someone who has attained the first absorption, speech has ceased. …

segs.p: khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno rāgo niruddho hoti, doso niruddho hoti, moho niruddho hoti.
segs.e: For a mendicant who has ended the defilements, greed, hate, and delusion have ceased.

segs.p: Atha kho pana, bhikkhave, mayā anupubbasaṅkhārānaṁ vūpasamo akkhāto.
segs.e: And I have also explained the progressive settling of activities.

segs.p: Paṭhamaṁ jhānaṁ samāpannassa vācā vūpasantā hoti …pe…
segs.e: For someone who has attained the first absorption, speech has stilled. …

segs.p: khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno rāgo vūpasanto hoti, doso vūpasanto hoti, moho vūpasanto hoti.
segs.e: For a mendicant who has ended the defilements, greed, hate, and delusion have stilled.
There are these six levels of tranquility.

segs.p: Paṭhamaṁ jhānaṁ samāpannassa vācā paṭippassaddhā hoti.
segs.e: For someone who has attained the first absorption, speech has been tranquilized.

segs.p: Dutiyaṁ jhānaṁ samāpannassa vitakkavicārā paṭippassaddhā honti.
segs.e: For someone who has attained the second absorption, the placing of the mind and keeping it connected have been tranquilized.

segs.p: Tatiyaṁ jhānaṁ samāpannassa pīti paṭippassaddhā hoti.
segs.e: For someone who has attained the third absorption, rapture has been tranquilized.

segs.p: Catutthaṁ jhānaṁ samāpannassa assāsapassāsā paṭippassaddhā honti.
segs.e: For someone who has attained the fourth absorption, breathing has been tranquilized.

segs.p: Saññāvedayitanirodhaṁ samāpannassa saññā ca vedanā ca paṭippassaddhā honti.
segs.e: For someone who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, perception and feeling have been tranquilized.

segs.p: Khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno rāgo paṭippassaddho hoti, doso paṭippassaddho hoti, moho paṭippassaddho hotī”ti.
segs.e: For a mendicant who has ended the defilements, greed, hate, and delusion have been tranquilized.”

With Several Mendicants (2nd)

2. In Private
With Pañcakaṅga

segs.p: Atha kho pañcakaṅgo thapati yenāyasmā udāyī tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṁ udāyiṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho pañcakaṅgo thapati āyasmantaṁ udāyiṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then the chamberlain Pañcakaṅga went up to Venerable Udāyī, bowed, sat down to one side, and asked him,

segs.p: “kati nu kho, bhante udāyi, vedanā vuttā bhagavatā”ti?
segs.e: “Sir, how many feelings has the Buddha spoken of?”
“Chamberlain, the Buddha has spoken of three feelings:

segs.p: Sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā—
segs.e: pleasant, painful, and neutral.

segs.p: imā kho, thapati, tisso vedanā vuttā bhagavatā”ti.
segs.e: The Buddha has spoken of these three feelings.”

segs.p: Evaṁ vutte, pañcakaṅgo thapati āyasmantaṁ udāyiṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: When he said this, Pañcakaṅga said to Udāyī,

segs.p: “na kho, bhante udāyi, tisso vedanā vuttā bhagavatā.
segs.e: “Sir, Udāyī, the Buddha hasn’t spoken of three feelings.
He’s spoken of two feelings:
pleasant and painful.

segs.p: Yāyaṁ, bhante, adukkhamasukhā vedanā, santasmiṁ esā paṇīte sukhe vuttā bhagavatā”ti.
segs.e: The Buddha said that neutral feeling is included as a peaceful and subtle kind of pleasure.”

segs.p: Dutiyampi kho āyasmā udāyī pañcakaṅgaṁ thapatiṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: For a second time, Udāyī said to him,

segs.p: “na kho, thapati, dve vedanā vuttā bhagavatā.
segs.e: “The Buddha hasn’t spoken of two feelings,
he’s spoken of three.”

segs.p: Sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā—
Dutiyampi kho pañcakaṅgo thapati āyasmantaṁ udāyiṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: For a second time, Pañcakaṅga said to Udāyī,

segs.p: “na kho, bhante udāyi, tisso vedanā vuttā bhagavatā.
segs.e: “The Buddha hasn’t spoken of three feelings,
he’s spoken of two.”

segs.p: Yāyaṁ, bhante, adukkhamasukhā vedanā, santasmiṁ esā paṇīte sukhe vuttā bhagavatā”ti.
Tatiyampi kho āyasmā udāyī pañcakaṅgaṁ thapatiṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: And for a third time, Udāyī said to him,

segs.p: “na kho, thapati, dve vedanā vuttā bhagavatā.
segs.e: “The Buddha hasn’t spoken of two feelings,
he’s spoken of three.”

segs.p: Sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā—
Tatiyampi kho pañcakaṅgo thapati āyasmantaṁ udāyiṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: And for a third time, Pañcakaṅga said to Udāyī,

segs.p: “na kho, bhante udāyi, tisso vedanā vuttā bhagavatā.
segs.e: “The Buddha hasn’t spoken of three feelings,
he’s spoken of two.”

segs.p: Yāyaṁ, bhante, adukkhamasukhā vedanā, santasmiṁ esā paṇīte sukhe vuttā bhagavatā”ti.
Neva sakkhi āyasmā udāyī pañcakaṅgaṁ thapatiṁ saññāpetuṁ, na panāsakkhi pañcakaṅgo thapati āyasmantaṁ udāyiṁ saññāpetuṁ.
segs.e: But neither was able to persuade the other.

segs.p: Assosi kho āyasmā ānando āyasmato udāyissa pañcakaṅgena thapatinā saddhiṁ imaṁ kathāsallāpaṁ.
segs.e: Venerable Ānanda heard this discussion between Udāyī and Pañcakaṅga.

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā ānando yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi.
segs.e: He went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side,

segs.p: Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho āyasmā ānando yāvatako āyasmato udāyissa pañcakaṅgena thapatinā saddhiṁ ahosi kathāsallāpo taṁ sabbaṁ bhagavato ārocesi.
segs.e: and informed the Buddha of all they had discussed.

segs.p: “Santameva, ānanda, pariyāyaṁ pañcakaṅgo thapati udāyissa bhikkhuno nābbhanumodi;
segs.e: “Ānanda, the explanation by the mendicant Udāyī, which the chamberlain Pañcakaṅga didn’t agree with, was quite correct.

segs.p: santañca panānanda, pariyāyaṁ udāyī bhikkhu pañcakaṅgassa thapatino nābbhanumodi.
segs.e: But the explanation by Pañcakaṅga, which Udāyī didn’t agree with, was also quite correct.

segs.p: Dvepi mayā, ānanda, vedanā vuttā pariyāyena.
segs.e: In one explanation I’ve spoken of two feelings. In another explanation I’ve spoken of three feelings, or five, six, eighteen, thirty-six, or a hundred and eight feelings.

segs.p: Evaṁ pariyāyadesito kho, ānanda, mayā dhammo.
segs.e: I’ve explained the teaching in all these different ways.

segs.p: Evaṁ pariyāyadesite kho, ānanda, mayā dhamme ye aññamaññassa subhāsitaṁ sulapitaṁ, na samanumaññissanti, na samanujānissanti, na samanumodissanti, tesaṁ etaṁ pāṭikaṅkhaṁ—bhaṇḍanajātā kalahajātā vivādāpannā aññamaññaṁ mukhasattīhi vitudantā viharissantīti.
segs.e: This being so, you can expect that those who don’t concede, approve, or agree with what has been well spoken will fight, quarrel, and dispute, continually wounding each other with barbed words.

segs.p: Evaṁ pariyāyadesito kho, ānanda, mayā dhammo.
segs.e: I’ve explained the teaching in all these different ways.

segs.p: Evaṁ pariyāyadesite kho, ānanda, mayā dhamme ye aññamaññassa subhāsitaṁ sulapitaṁ samanumaññissanti samanujānissanti samanumodissanti, tesaṁ etaṁ pāṭikaṅkhaṁ—samaggā sammodamānā avivadamānā khīrodakībhūtā aññamaññaṁ piyacakkhūhi sampassantā viharissantīti.
segs.e: This being so, you can expect that those who do concede, approve, or agree with what has been well spoken will live in harmony, appreciating each other, without dispute, blending like milk and water, and regarding each other with kindly eyes.
There are these five kinds of sensual stimulation.
What five?

segs.p: Cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṁhitā rajanīyā …pe…
segs.e: Sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing. …

segs.p: kāyaviññeyyā phoṭṭhabbā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṁhitā rajanīyā.
segs.e: Touches known by the body, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.
These are the five kinds of sensual stimulation.

segs.p: Yaṁ kho, ānanda, ime pañca kāmaguṇe paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṁ somanassaṁ—
segs.e: The pleasure and happiness that arise from these five kinds of sensual stimulation is called sensual pleasure.
There are those who might say
that this is the highest pleasure and happiness that sentient beings experience.
But I don’t grant them that.
Why is that?

segs.p: Atthānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṁ sukhaṁ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca.
segs.e: Because there is another pleasure that is finer than that.

segs.p: Katamañcānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṁ sukhaṁ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca?
segs.e: And what is that pleasure?

segs.p: Idhānanda, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṁ savicāraṁ vivekajaṁ pītisukhaṁ paṭhamaṁ jhānaṁ upasampajja viharati.
segs.e: It’s when a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

segs.p: Idaṁ kho, ānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṁ sukhaṁ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca.
segs.e: This is a pleasure that is finer than that.
There are those who might say
that this is the highest pleasure and happiness that sentient beings experience.
But I don’t grant them that.
Why is that?

segs.p: Atthānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṁ sukhaṁ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca.
segs.e: Because there is another pleasure that is finer than that.

segs.p: Katamañcānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṁ sukhaṁ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca?
segs.e: And what is that pleasure?

segs.p: Idhānanda, bhikkhu, vitakkavicārānaṁ vūpasamā ajjhattaṁ sampasādanaṁ cetaso ekodibhāvaṁ avitakkaṁ avicāraṁ samādhijaṁ pītisukhaṁ dutiyaṁ jhānaṁ upasampajja viharati.
segs.e: It’s when, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, a mendicant enters and remains in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

segs.p: Idaṁ kho, ānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṁ sukhaṁ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca.
segs.e: This is a pleasure that is finer than that.
There are those who might say
that this is the highest pleasure and happiness that sentient beings experience.
But I don’t grant them that.
Why is that?

segs.p: Atthānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṁ sukhaṁ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca.
segs.e: Because there is another pleasure that is finer than that.

segs.p: Katamañcānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṁ sukhaṁ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca?
segs.e: And what is that pleasure?

segs.p: Idhānanda, bhikkhu pītiyā ca virāgā upekkhako ca viharati sato ca sampajāno, sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṁvedeti, yaṁ taṁ ariyā ācikkhanti: ‘upekkhako satimā sukhavihārī’ti tatiyaṁ jhānaṁ upasampajja viharati.
segs.e: It’s when, with the fading away of rapture, a mendicant enters and remains in the third absorption, where they meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’

segs.p: Idaṁ kho, ānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṁ sukhaṁ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca.
segs.e: This is a pleasure that is finer than that.
There are those who might say
that this is the highest pleasure and happiness that sentient beings experience.
But I don’t grant them that.
Why is that?

segs.p: Atthānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṁ sukhaṁ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca.
segs.e: Because there is another pleasure that is finer than that.

segs.p: Katamañcānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṁ sukhaṁ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca?
segs.e: And what is that pleasure?

segs.p: Idhānanda, bhikkhu sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānā pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṁ atthaṅgamā adukkhamasukhaṁ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṁ catutthaṁ jhānaṁ upasampajja viharati.
segs.e: It’s when, with the giving up of pleasure and pain and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, a mendicant enters and remains in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.

segs.p: Idaṁ kho, ānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṁ sukhaṁ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca.
segs.e: This is a pleasure that is finer than that.
There are those who might say
that this is the highest pleasure and happiness that sentient beings experience.
But I don’t grant them that.
Why is that?

segs.p: Atthānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṁ sukhaṁ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca.
segs.e: Because there is another pleasure that is finer than that.

segs.p: Katamañcānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṁ sukhaṁ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca?
segs.e: And what is that pleasure?

segs.p: Idhānanda, bhikkhu sabbaso rūpasaññānaṁ samatikkamā, paṭighasaññānaṁ atthaṅgamā, nānattasaññānaṁ amanasikārā, ‘ananto ākāso’ti ākāsānañcāyatanaṁ upasampajja viharati.
segs.e: It’s when a mendicant, going totally beyond perceptions of form, with the ending of perceptions of impingement, not focusing on perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite’, enters and remains in the dimension of infinite space.

segs.p: Idaṁ kho, ānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṁ sukhaṁ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca.
segs.e: This is a pleasure that is finer than that.
There are those who might say
that this is the highest pleasure and happiness that sentient beings experience.
But I don’t grant them that.
Why is that?

segs.e: It’s when a mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite’, enters and remains in the dimension of infinite consciousness.

segs.p: Idaṁ kho, ānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṁ sukhaṁ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca.

segs.e: It’s when a mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of nothingness, enters and remains in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception.

segs.p: Idhānanda, bhikkhu sabbaso nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṁ samatikkamma saññāvedayitanirodhaṁ upasampajja viharati.
segs.e: It’s when a mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, enters and remains in the cessation of perception and feeling.

segs.p: Idaṁ kho, ānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṁ sukhaṁ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca.

A Mendicant

segs.p: “Dvepi mayā, bhikkhave, vedanā vuttā pariyāyena, tissopi mayā vedanā vuttā pariyāyena, pañcapi mayā vedanā vuttā pariyāyena, chapi mayā vedanā vuttā pariyāyena, aṭṭhārasāpi mayā vedanā vuttā pariyāyena, chattiṁsāpi mayā vedanā vuttā pariyāyena, aṭṭhasatampi mayā vedanā vuttā pariyāyena.

segs.p: Evaṁ pariyāyadesite kho, bhikkhave, mayā dhamme ye aññamaññassa subhāsitaṁ sulapitaṁ na samanumaññissanti, na samanujānissanti, na samanumodissanti, tesaṁ etaṁ pāṭikaṅkhaṁ—bhaṇḍanajātā kalahajātā vivādāpannā aññamaññaṁ mukhasattīhi vitudantā viharissantīti.

3. The Explanation of the Hundred and Eight
With Sīvaka

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā rājagahe viharati veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

segs.p: Atha kho moḷiyasīvako paribbājako yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavatā saddhiṁ sammodi.
segs.e: Then the wanderer Moḷiyasīvaka went up to the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him.

segs.p: Sammodanīyaṁ kathaṁ sāraṇīyaṁ vītisāretvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho moḷiyasīvako paribbājako bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to the Buddha:

segs.p: “santi, bho gotama, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṁvādino evaṁdiṭṭhino:
segs.e: “Worthy Gotama, there are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view:

segs.p: ‘yaṁ kiñcāyaṁ purisapuggalo paṭisaṁvedeti sukhaṁ vā dukkhaṁ vā adukkhamasukhaṁ vā sabbaṁ taṁ pubbekatahetū’ti.
segs.e: ‘Everything this individual person experiences—pleasurable, painful, or neutral—is because of past deeds.’
What does the worthy Gotama say about this?”
“Sīvaka, some feelings stem from bile disorders.

segs.p: Sāmampi kho etaṁ, sīvaka, veditabbaṁ yathā pittasamuṭṭhānānipi idhekaccāni vedayitāni uppajjanti.

segs.e: and it is generally deemed to be true.

segs.p: Tatra, sīvaka, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṁvādino evaṁdiṭṭhino:
segs.e: Since this is so, the ascetics and brahmins whose view is that

segs.p: ‘yaṁ kiñcāyaṁ purisapuggalo paṭisaṁvedeti sukhaṁ vā dukkhaṁ vā adukkhamasukhaṁ vā sabbaṁ taṁ pubbekatahetū’ti.

segs.p: Yañca sāmaṁ ñātaṁ tañca atidhāvanti, yañca loke saccasammataṁ tañca atidhāvanti.

wind disorders …

segs.p: kammavipākajānipi kho, sīvaka, idhekaccāni vedayitāni uppajjanti.

segs.p: upāsakaṁ maṁ bhavaṁ gotamo dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṁ saraṇaṁ gatan”ti.

3. The Explanation of the Hundred and Eight
The Explanation of the Hundred and Eight
“Mendicants, I will teach you an exposition of the teaching on the hundred and eight.
Listen …
And what is the exposition of the teaching on the hundred and eight?

segs.p: Dvepi mayā, bhikkhave, vedanā vuttā pariyāyena;
segs.e: Mendicants, in one explanation I’ve spoken of two feelings. In another explanation I’ve spoken of three feelings, or five, six, eighteen, thirty-six, or a hundred and eight feelings.
And what are the two feelings?
Physical and mental.
These are called the two feelings.
And what are the three feelings?

segs.p: Sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā—
segs.e: Pleasant, painful, and neutral feelings. …
And what are the five feelings?
The faculties of pleasure, pain, happiness, sadness, and equanimity. …
And what are the six feelings?
Feeling born of eye contact … ear contact … nose contact … tongue contact … body contact …
mind contact. …
And what are the eighteen feelings?

segs.p: Cha somanassūpavicārā, cha domanassūpavicārā, cha upekkhūpavicārā—
segs.e: There are six preoccupations with happiness, six preoccupations with sadness, and six preoccupations with equanimity. …
And what are the thirty-six feelings?

segs.p: Cha gehasitāni somanassāni, cha nekkhammasitāni somanassāni, cha gehasitāni domanassāni, cha nekkhammasitāni domanassāni, cha gehasitā upekkhā, cha nekkhammasitā upekkhā—
segs.e: Six kinds of domestic happiness and six kinds of renunciate happiness. Six kinds of domestic sadness and six kinds of renunciate sadness. Six kinds of domestic equanimity and six kinds of renunciate equanimity. …
And what are the hundred and eight feelings?

segs.p: Atītā chattiṁsa vedanā, anāgatā chattiṁsa vedanā, paccuppannā chattiṁsa vedanā—
segs.e: Thirty six feelings in the past, future, and present.
These are called the hundred and eight feelings.
This is the exposition of the teaching on the hundred and eight.”

3. The Explanation of the Hundred and Eight
With a Mendicant

segs.p: Atha kho aññataro bhikkhu yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho so bhikkhu bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then a mendicant went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

segs.p: “katamā nu kho, bhante, vedanā, katamo vedanāsamudayo, katamā vedanāsamudayagāminī paṭipadā?
segs.e: “Sir, what is feeling? What’s the origin of feeling? What’s the practice that leads to the origin of feeling?
What’s the cessation of feeling? What’s the practice that leads to the cessation of feeling?

segs.p: Ko vedanāya assādo, ko ādīnavo, kiṁ nissaraṇan”ti?
segs.e: And what is feeling’s gratification, drawback, and escape?”
“Mendicant, there are these three feelings:

segs.p: sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā.
segs.e: pleasant, painful, and neutral.
These are called feelings.
Feeling originates from contact.
Craving is the practice that leads to the origin of feeling.
When contact ceases, feeling ceases.

segs.p: Ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo vedanānirodhagāminī paṭipadā, seyyathidaṁ—
segs.e: The practice that leads to the cessation of feelings is simply this noble eightfold path, that is:
right view, right purpose, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion.

segs.p: Yaṁ vedanaṁ paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṁ somanassaṁ, ayaṁ vedanāya assādo;
segs.e: The pleasure and happiness that arise from feeling: this is its gratification.

segs.p: yaṁ vedanā aniccā dukkhā vipariṇāmadhammā, ayaṁ vedanāya ādīnavo;
segs.e: That feeling is impermanent, suffering, and perishable: this is its drawback.

segs.p: yo vedanāya chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānaṁ, idaṁ vedanāya nissaraṇan”ti.
segs.e: Removing and giving up desire and greed for feeling: this is its escape.”

3. The Explanation of the Hundred and Eight
Before

segs.p: “Pubbeva me, bhikkhave, sambodhā anabhisambuddhassa bodhisattasseva sato etadahosi:
segs.e: “Mendicants, before my awakening—when I was still unawakened but intent on awakening—I thought:

segs.p: ‘katamā nu kho vedanā, katamo vedanāsamudayo, katamā vedanāsamudayagāminī paṭipadā, katamo vedanānirodho, katamā vedanānirodhagāminī paṭipadā?

segs.p: Ko vedanāya assādo, ko ādīnavo, kiṁ nissaraṇan’ti?

Then it occurred to me:

segs.p: sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā.
segs.e: pleasant, painful, and neutral.
These are called feelings.

segs.p: yo vedanāya chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānaṁ. Idaṁ vedanāya nissaraṇan’”ti.
segs.e: Removing and giving up desire and greed for feeling: this is its escape.’”

3. The Explanation of the Hundred and Eight
Ascetics and Brahmins (1st)
“Mendicants, there are these three feelings.
What three?

segs.p: Sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā.
segs.e: Pleasant, painful, and neutral feeling.

segs.p: Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā imāsaṁ tissannaṁ vedanānaṁ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṁ nappajānanti.
segs.e: There are ascetics and brahmins who don’t truly understand these three feelings’ gratification, drawback, and escape.

segs.p: Na me te, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā samaṇesu vā samaṇasammatā brāhmaṇesu vā brāhmaṇasammatā, na ca pana te āyasmanto sāmaññatthaṁ vā brahmaññatthaṁ vā diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṁ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharanti.
segs.e: I don’t deem them as true ascetics and brahmins. Those venerables don’t realize the goal of life as an ascetic or brahmin, and don’t live having realized it with their own insight in this very life.

segs.p: Ye ca kho keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā imāsaṁ tissannaṁ vedanānaṁ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṁ pajānanti.
segs.e: There are ascetics and brahmins who do truly understand these three feelings’ gratification, drawback, and escape.

segs.p: Te kho me, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā samaṇesu ceva samaṇasammatā brāhmaṇesu ca brāhmaṇasammatā. Te ca panāyasmanto sāmaññatthañca brahmaññatthañca, diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṁ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharantī”ti.
segs.e: I deem them as true ascetics and brahmins. Those venerables realize the goal of life as an ascetic or brahmin, and live having realized it with their own insight.”

3. The Explanation of the Hundred and Eight
Not of the Flesh

segs.p: “Atthi, bhikkhave, sāmisā pīti, atthi nirāmisā pīti, atthi nirāmisā nirāmisatarā pīti;
segs.e: “Mendicants, there is rapture of the flesh, rapture not  of the flesh, and rapture even more spiritual than that not of the flesh.

segs.p: atthi sāmisaṁ sukhaṁ, atthi nirāmisaṁ sukhaṁ, atthi nirāmisā nirāmisataraṁ sukhaṁ;
segs.e: There is pleasure of the flesh, pleasure not of the flesh, and pleasure even more spiritual than that not of the flesh.

segs.p: atthi sāmisā upekkhā, atthi nirāmisā upekkhā, atthi nirāmisā nirāmisatarā upekkhā;
segs.e: There is equanimity of the flesh, equanimity not of the flesh, and equanimity even more spiritual than that not of the flesh.

segs.p: atthi sāmiso vimokkho, atthi nirāmiso vimokkho, atthi nirāmisā nirāmisataro vimokkho.
segs.e: There is liberation of the flesh, liberation not of the flesh, and liberation even more spiritual than that not of the flesh.
And what is rapture of the flesh?
There are these five kinds of sensual stimulation.
What five?

segs.p: Cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṁhitā rajanīyā …pe…
segs.e: Sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing. Sounds … Smells … Tastes …

segs.p: kāyaviññeyyā phoṭṭhabbā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṁhitā rajanīyā.
segs.e: Touches known by the body, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.
These are the five kinds of sensual stimulation.

segs.p: Yā kho, bhikkhave, ime pañca kāmaguṇe paṭicca uppajjati pīti, ayaṁ vuccati, bhikkhave, sāmisā pīti.
segs.e: The rapture that arises from these five kinds of sensual stimulation is called rapture of the flesh.
And what is rapture not of the flesh?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṁ savicāraṁ vivekajaṁ pītisukhaṁ paṭhamaṁ jhānaṁ upasampajja viharati.
segs.e: It’s when a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

segs.p: Vitakkavicārānaṁ vūpasamā ajjhattaṁ sampasādanaṁ cetaso ekodibhāvaṁ avitakkaṁ avicāraṁ samādhijaṁ pītisukhaṁ dutiyaṁ jhānaṁ upasampajja viharati.
segs.e: As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, they enter and remain in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.
This is called rapture not of the flesh.

segs.p: Katamā ca, bhikkhave, nirāmisā nirāmisatarā pīti?
segs.e: And what is rapture even more spiritual than that not of the flesh?

segs.p: Yā kho, bhikkhave, khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno rāgā cittaṁ vimuttaṁ paccavekkhato, dosā cittaṁ vimuttaṁ paccavekkhato, mohā cittaṁ vimuttaṁ paccavekkhato uppajjati pīti, ayaṁ vuccati, bhikkhave, nirāmisā nirāmisatarā pīti.
segs.e: When a mendicant who has ended the defilements reviews their mind free from greed, hate, and delusion, rapture arises. This is called rapture even more spiritual than that not of the flesh.
And what is pleasure of the flesh?
Mendicants, there are these five kinds of sensual stimulation.
What five?

segs.p: Cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṁhitā rajanīyā …pe…
segs.e: Sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing. Sounds … Smells … Tastes …

segs.p: kāyaviññeyyā phoṭṭhabbā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṁhitā rajanīyā.
segs.e: Touches known by the body, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.
These are the five kinds of sensual stimulation.

segs.p: Yaṁ kho, bhikkhave, ime pañca kāmaguṇe paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṁ somanassaṁ, idaṁ vuccati, bhikkhave, sāmisaṁ sukhaṁ.
segs.e: The pleasure and happiness that arise from these five kinds of sensual stimulation is called pleasure of the flesh.
And what is pleasure not of the flesh?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṁ savicāraṁ vivekajaṁ pītisukhaṁ paṭhamaṁ jhānaṁ upasampajja viharati.
segs.e: It’s when a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.

segs.p: Vitakkavicārānaṁ vūpasamā ajjhattaṁ sampasādanaṁ cetaso ekodibhāvaṁ avitakkaṁ avicāraṁ samādhijaṁ pītisukhaṁ dutiyaṁ jhānaṁ upasampajja viharati.
segs.e: As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, they enter and remain in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected.

segs.p: Pītiyā ca virāgā upekkhako ca viharati sato ca sampajāno sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṁvedeti, yaṁ taṁ ariyā ācikkhanti: ‘upekkhako satimā sukhavihārī’ti tatiyaṁ jhānaṁ upasampajja viharati.
segs.e: And with the fading away of rapture, they enter and remain in the third absorption, where they meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, experiencing for themselves the bliss of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.’
This is called pleasure not of the flesh.
And what is pleasure even more spiritual than that not of the flesh?

segs.p: Yaṁ kho, bhikkhave, khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno rāgā cittaṁ vimuttaṁ paccavekkhato, dosā cittaṁ vimuttaṁ paccavekkhato, mohā cittaṁ vimuttaṁ paccavekkhato uppajjati sukhaṁ somanassaṁ, idaṁ vuccati, bhikkhave, nirāmisā nirāmisataraṁ sukhaṁ.
segs.e: When a mendicant who has ended the defilements reviews their mind free from greed, hate, and delusion, pleasure and happiness arises. This is called pleasure even more spiritual than that not of the flesh.
And what is equanimity of the flesh?
There are these five kinds of sensual stimulation.
What five?

segs.p: Cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṁhitā rajanīyā …pe…
segs.e: Sights known by the eye, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing. Sounds … Smells … Tastes …

segs.p: kāyaviññeyyā phoṭṭhabbā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṁhitā rajanīyā.
segs.e: Touches known by the body, which are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing.
These are the five kinds of sensual stimulation.

segs.p: Yā kho, bhikkhave, ime pañca kāmaguṇe paṭicca uppajjati upekkhā, ayaṁ vuccati, bhikkhave, sāmisā upekkhā.
segs.e: The equanimity that arises from these five kinds of sensual stimulation is called equanimity of the flesh.
And what is equanimity not of the flesh?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sukhassa ca pahānā, dukkhassa ca pahānā, pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṁ atthaṅgamā, adukkhamasukhaṁ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṁ catutthaṁ jhānaṁ upasampajja viharati.
segs.e: It’s when, with the giving up of pleasure and pain and the disappearance of former happiness and sadness, a mendicant enters and remains in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness.
This is called equanimity not of the flesh.

segs.p: Katamā ca, bhikkhave, nirāmisā nirāmisatarā upekkhā?
segs.e: And what is equanimity even more spiritual than that not of the flesh?

segs.p: Yā kho, bhikkhave, khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno rāgā cittaṁ vimuttaṁ paccavekkhato, dosā cittaṁ vimuttaṁ paccavekkhato, mohā cittaṁ vimuttaṁ paccavekkhato uppajjati upekkhā, ayaṁ vuccati, bhikkhave, nirāmisā nirāmisatarā upekkhā.
segs.e: When a mendicant who has ended the defilements reviews their mind free from greed, hate, and delusion, equanimity arises. This is called equanimity even more spiritual than that not of the flesh.
And what is liberation of the flesh?
Liberation connected with form is liberation of the flesh.
And what is liberation not of the flesh?
Liberation connected with the formless is liberation not of the flesh.

segs.p: Katamo ca, bhikkhave, nirāmisā nirāmisataro vimokkho?
segs.e: And what is liberation even more spiritual than that not of the flesh?

segs.p: Yo kho, bhikkhave, khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno rāgā cittaṁ vimuttaṁ paccavekkhato, dosā cittaṁ vimuttaṁ paccavekkhato, mohā cittaṁ vimuttaṁ paccavekkhato uppajjati vimokkho, ayaṁ vuccati, bhikkhave, nirāmisā nirāmisataro vimokkho”ti.
segs.e: When a mendicant who has ended the defilements reviews their mind free from greed, hate, and delusion, liberation arises. This is called liberation even more spiritual than that not of the flesh.”
